title: About 60,000 migrants arrive in Ceuta in 24 hours, Spanish territory's leader says
description: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the French president offered to help Spain.Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, is separated from mainland Spain by
body: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and the French president offered to help Spain.Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar and has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.Local officials had appealed to Madrid for help after a recent rise in attempted crossings, but there were chaotic scenes on Thursday as border controls apparently broke down.Ceuta's President Juan Jesús Vivas said the situation was "unsustainable" and that the recent arrivals amounted to around 70% of the city's population - which sits at around 83,600 according to the latest local figures.Spain's Interior Ministry told the BBC that its estimates were slightly lower, citing 50,000 arrivals since the early hours of Thursday.It also added that more than 25,000 people have left Ceuta en route back to Morocco from Friday morning up to 13:00 local time (11:00 GMT).The ministry said the rate of departures from Ceuta is at 150 people per minute, though it did not provide any further information on this.Spain has now deployed its armed forces to bolster security in Ceuta and at its sister city of Melilla, where between 300 to 400 crossings were also reported overnight.Speaking on Friday during a visit to Ceuta, Sánchez said that the government would be looking at reinforcing the border with Morocco. He blamed criminal networks for manipulating the Supreme Court's recent ruling, adding that incorrect information had "spread like wildfire in recent hours".He said authorities in Morocco were co-operating with plans to return those who had entered illegally. Ceuta and Melilla trace their Spanish past to the 15th Century, and they have enjoyed a limited degree of self-government since 1995.Coveted by Morocco, they have long been a flashpoint in diplomatic relations between the two countries. They form the European Union's only land borders with Africa.One migrant told Reuters news agency that he was returning to Morocco, adding:"It's not good at all, and it's not fun either."I mean, people are dying here. I beg you, please, if you haven't come yet, don't come. Don't do it."Local media reported chaos on the streets of Ceuta since Thursday, with one resident telling Spain's ABC that people were scared."Nobody is going out on the street. They're afraid."This is stronger and more aggressive than what we've experienced before," a hospital security guard told the Spanish site.The last time there was a surge in arrivals - though on nowhere near this scale - was in 2021. At that point, the Moroccan authorities allowed some 8,000 people to cross the border following a dispute with Madrid over the sovereignty of the Western Sahara.That diplomatic dispute has flared again recently, after Sánchez travelled to Algeria which backs independence for the region.BBC Verify has looked into migration data released by the UN, external, which reported 2,826 people had crossed into Ceuta up until 15 July this year with another 181 entering via Melilla.The number of migrants crossing into these two territories was already high compared with recent years, which saw 994 migrants enter in 2025, 476 in 2024 and 467 in 2023.

schema.headline: About 60,000 migrants arrive in Ceuta in 24 hours, Spanish territory's leader says

title: Anthropic's Claude AI escapes tests to hack three organisations
description: US technology firm Anthropic says its AI models hacked into the systems of three organisations on their own, during a private security experiment.The
body: US technology firm Anthropic says its AI models hacked into the systems of three organisations on their own, during a private security experiment.The models found a weakness in what was supposed to be an isolated test environment and connected to the internet.It comes just days after rival OpenAI said that its models had breached the systems of other companies, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.The announcement prompted Anthropic to check whether its own systems had carried out similar attacks. It says it uncovered three cases which have since been reported to the affected companies.Anthropic, which did not name the organisations, urged other AI labs to perform similar reviews to better understand the risks of their models' capabilities.Anthropic said in a statement, external it reviewed more than 140,000 tests to find evidence Claude - its family of AI models - had managed to get online even though it was supposed to be in an isolated test environment, cut off from the internet.The tests included exercises in which Claude was tasked with obtaining "secret" information hidden on another machine on the closed-off network.It was then told to get the information by breaking into the machine and finding it - a common way that experts assess a model's hacking capabilities.A "misconfiguration" on systems run by Anthropic and its testing partner left the models with live internet access.Treating it all as still part of the same exercise, Claude then connected to the internet and breached the systems of three real organisations rather than just test ones, the San Francisco-based firm said.Anthropic said the earliest incidents date back to April and that it is "approaching the fixes as if the responsibility were ours alone."Neither Anthropic nor the organisations that were breached had noticed the intrusions at the time. Anthropic said it could have reviewed its records more thoroughly and added that the findings gave the firm "cautious optimism" that such risks can be overcome with more investment and tighter measures.Professor Gina Neff, head of the Minderoo Centre at the University of Cambridge, said the review showed "AI models doing what people told them to"."The moral of this story is not to fear robots that will take over, but the companies behind powerful AI agents who are making the decisions about what is safe for the rest of us," she said."It also shows why independent testing and government oversight is crucial."Meanwhile, cyber-security expert David Allott from Veeam Software told the BBC the lesson to take from the cyber-attacks was "not necessarily that AI has developed a fundamentally new attack capability"."Instead, it is that AI agents can combine capabilities, obtain credentials and system access to take actions autonomously, while adapting scope and scale at machine speed," he said.The incidents come as tech firms pour billions of dollars into developing AI agents that can independently perform tasks ranging from research and customer support to cyber-security.

schema.headline: Anthropic's Claude AI escapes tests to hack three organisations

title: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show how UK landscape has changed
description: Dr Jess Neumann, an associate professor at the University of Reading, said while it is not unusual to see some browning in the summer, the "large expa
body: Dr Jess Neumann, an associate professor at the University of Reading, said while it is not unusual to see some browning in the summer, the "large expanses of dry grass in parks, lawns and gardens" are particularly noticeable this year.Neumann added that British plants are "not adapted to prolonged summer droughts and hot weather", unlike in places like the Mediterranean.This summer's "flash" drought is also notable for how quickly it has developed, given in early spring river flows, soil moisture and reservoir levels were generally around or above normal following a very wet start to 2026.The recent repeated heatwaves have sapped moisture from soils and vegetation via evaporation, which has in turn increased demand for water for farming, industry and household use."The drought could have a direct knock-on effect on food supplies," said Dr Pauline Scheelbeek, associate professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.She added that it is possible there will be "less British produce and at higher prices in our supermarkets" because less reliable access to water may reduce crop yields.Another impact on UK agriculture is low grass stocks forcing some farmers to use winter feed for their livestock during the summer leaving supplies short for later in the year.Prof Michael Singer from Cardiff University has expressed concern about the effect on wildlife, as "many animals and plants in the UK are not well adapted to extreme drought conditions."

schema.headline: UK heatwaves: Satellite images show how UK landscape has changed

title: UK petrol prices hit highest level since Iran war began
description: Image source, Maskot/Getty ImagesUpdated 2 hours agoUK petrol prices have risen to their highest level since the beginning of the Iran war as the conf
body: Image source, Maskot/Getty ImagesUpdated 2 hours agoUK petrol prices have risen to their highest level since the beginning of the Iran war as the conflict continues to hit drivers' finances.The average cost of petrol has reached 160p per litre, according to motoring group the RAC.The price of fuel tends to track the wholesale price of oil, which surged when the Iran conflict began on 28 February as the fighting severely disrupted oil supplies across the Middle East.Prices then nosedived when US and Iran agreed to a framework deal to end the conflict in June, but they have risen again since the collapse of peace talks.How do wholesale oil prices affect the cost of petrol and diesel at the pump?Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive.Analysts say every $10 (£7.44) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre.Since the war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices – has been very volatile.Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down.Before the conflict, Brent was about $70 a barrel, but the fighting saw it peak at above $120.  In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 a barrel mark.When the peace talks collapsed, the price climbed back up again to above $100 a barrel, but are now around $90.What has happened to petrol and diesel prices in the UK?While petrol has hit its highest price since the Iran war began, according to the RAC, diesel remains below the peak of 191.54p a litre it reached on 15 April.In early July, the RAC said the average price of petrol sank to a low of 150.59p per litre and 164.52p per litre for diesel.Since then the prices have risen, with petrol now at 159.97p a litre while diesel costs 178.97p a litre.RAC head of policy Simon Williams said the price of diesel was likely to reach 185p a litre "in the next few weeks, barring any major oil price reduction".Despite the conflict, petrol and diesel prices remain below the levels reached in the summer of 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, when petrol reached 191.5p a litre and diesel hit 199p. Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in the wholesale markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump.Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis".A government scheme called Fuel Finder, external lets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK. Luke Bosdet, the head of policy at the AA, said the group had been surprised at the speed that prices had fallen and put it down to the scheme.On 20 May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said a planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponed until 31 December because of the conflict. Why has the Iran war had a big impact on oil prices?The Middle East conflict sent global oil prices soaring as it effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - one of the world's key water transport routes for oil, liquid natural gas and other essential commodities - limiting global supplies.About 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas normally passes through the waterway.Even if a deal is agreed to reopen the strait, experts warn it will take time before normal levels of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz resume, and the impact of the war will continue to affect the global economy for potentially months to come. Where does the UK get its oil and gas?The UK is heavily reliant on oil and gas imports, with the majority coming from the US and Norway.The price of oil on the global market determines how much the UK pays for it.Although the UK does get some oil from the North Sea, most of that is exported for refining elsewhere.You can also send us your questions by following this linkReporting by Faarea Masud, Jemma Crew, Alex Daniel, Michael Race, and Mitchell LabiakGet in touchHow have you been affected by the price rises? Share your experiencesGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: UK petrol prices hit highest level since Iran war began

title: Uefa boycott: Women's football 'first casualties' of Fifa's plans
description: Women's football will be the first to suffer if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors goes ahead,
body: Women's football will be the first to suffer if Fifa president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors goes ahead, according to former England defender Anita Asante.On Thursday European football's 55 member associations voted to boycott all Fifa competitions until the governing body drops Infantino's proposals.Uefa's stance will first be tested when the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup starts on 5 September in Poland."The first casualties will be women's football tournaments," Asante told BBC Sport."I don't think Fifa have considered the implications of their decision."The Polish Football Association (PZPN) said on Friday it has not received any information about teams withdrawing from the competition and preparations are continuing as planned.In October, England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have qualifiers for next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil. And the Under-17 Women's World Cup is scheduled to take place in October in Morocco."That's what's so frustrating for players. You can't take for granted the opportunity to play in the World Cup," said Asante."If this isn't resolved by the time of England's qualifiers, then the impact could be huge and it is already a busy schedule."Fifa and Infantino want to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).Infantino has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his controversial plans.In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".There is no mention in the document of the women's game.If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

schema.headline: Uefa boycott: Women's football 'first casualties' of Fifa's plans

title: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham will give all mayors of city regions in England a share of income tax revenue for the first time, as part of his drive to transfer power from Westminster to local leaders.Burnham will also allow English strategic authorities to keep some cash from business rates collected in their areas, and gain greater control over services such as housing, transport, skills.The government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get, with more details to be announced when Chancellor John Healey delivers his first budget in the autumn.Opposition parties said the plans lacked detail and could lead to areas with weaker economies losing out on funding.But Burnham said the move would "make good" on his pledge to "bring power home" to "every postcode in the country"."Under our plans, more of the taxes raised in a community will stay in that community," the prime minister added.First Secretary of State Louise Haigh told BBC Radio 4's Today programme areas without mayors would also benefit from investment because devolution powers would be held by new strategic authorities across England.Strategic authorities bring together local councils to control regional issues such as transport and economic development, with decisions taken collectively by council leaders rather than a single elected mayor.But Labour backbencher Perran Moon said the government's plans were "discriminatory" and could create a "two-tier system". The MP for Camborne and Redruth in Cornwall said the area would never have a mayor or become a combined authority and so risked not having access to devolved powers that other areas would have. "What we're asking government to do is to provide us with the same powers, the same funding that mayoral combined authorities have without the requirement of becoming a combined authority or having a mayor."The government has also announced that mayors will be given a fast-track route to building new tramways, roads and light rail in their areas. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the threshold at which local leaders need to seek approval for projects will rise to £500m, up from £200m. As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding by central government grants. Mayors are expected to start retaining some revenue from business rates from April 2027 and receive a portion of income tax from April 2028.The rates of income tax will not change as a result of the reform.Treasury sources say some metro mayors could end up with more money to spend if they grow their local economies and expand their tax bases, but officials are still figuring out how it will work in practice.One think tank, Re:State, has suggested, external the government should allocate mayors 2.5p in every pound raised by the 20p basic rate of income tax in their areas.Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said Burnham's announcement was "very short on the detail" with "no new money being announced", which could mean areas with weaker local economies could end up losing out.The Liberal Democrats warned the plans risked "creating a postcode lottery" that would leave millions of people living in rural areas "short-changed and underfunded".Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the prime minister should "fully devolve the power to stop the housing of illegal migrants in local communities by the Home Office".The power to raise and control tax revenues is highly centralised in the UK, making the country an outlier by international standards.The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD, external global policy forum.That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).During his time as Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham pushed for greater control over tax revenue, rather than having to rely on government grants.The UK government had already been exploring whether a share of revenue from national taxes could be distributed to metro mayors before Burnham became prime minister.Burnham has put devolution at the heart of his plan for government, arguing that metro mayors are best placed to boost economic growth across the country.Ministers will be expected to justify why powers should remain in Whitehall rather than being devolved, under a "local first" principle being developed by No 10 North in Manchester, with full details set to be published in a policy paper on the same date as the autumn budget.The government is also working out the details of an equalisation system to ensure areas where less tax is collected continue to receive financial support.The reforms come after a policy blitz during Burnham's first two weeks in Downing Street, with announcements on the cost of living followed by a speech on his plan to overhaul social care.Tracy Brabin, the Labour mayor of West Yorkshire, said that giving regions like hers a proportion of income tax would mean "people will be able to see and feel the real benefit of their hard work and where that money is going".However, Lord Houchen, the Conservative mayor for Tees Valley, said he would prefer the government to cut taxes and if handed a portion of income tax would create a new rebate scheme to give money back to local people. "The prime minister has said he wants to alleviate the cost of living [crisis] and give people room to breathe - what better way to do that than allow them to keep more of their own money?" he told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme."I think the prime minister and what this government is doing on fiscal devolution is a move in the right direction, but for it to be real devolution we've got to have local decision-making and choose what's best for the people we represent."He said it was "not beyond the wit of man" for a regional authority to be able to set up a rebate system, adding it would not be "overly complicated" and would not be particularly controversial.Burnham said the policy was "not about allowing mayors to become a sort of mini-chancellor" or "local home secretary". "This is a policy that is about growth and investment," he told LBC, adding that he was "misunderstanding the purpose of this". "They don't have to go for all of the things that are being suggested here, but, you know, we think these things will start to provide an answer to the low growth Britain has experienced over the last decade and more places start to see levels of growth that Greater Manchester has achieved."Additional reporting by Harry Farley, political correspondent, and James Gregory, political reporter.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham to give regional mayors share of income tax

title: World Cup 2026: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pedro Porro was one of four Spurs players still involved on the World Cup's final weekendByPrudent Nsengiyumv
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pedro Porro was one of four Spurs players still involved on the World Cup's final weekendByPrudent NsengiyumvaBBC Sport journalistThe Premier League season begins on 21 August - just 33 days after the World Cup final.For some clubs, that leaves barely enough time to welcome players back from the mandatory three-week post-tournament break required under Fifa regulations, let alone integrate them into pre-season preparations.Four Tottenham players were still involved on the final weekend of the tournament and may have little more than a week of training before the new campaign starts. Chelsea too were significantly affected.And Manchester City and Arsenal have their own concerns after seeing more players than any other Premier League club reach the latter stages of the competition.The World Cup may be over, but its impact on the Premier League is only just beginning.Spurs feel the impactTottenham are among the clubs whose pre-season preparations have been most significantly impacted.Cristian Romero and new signing Marcos Senesi reached the final with Argentina, while Pedro Porro helped Spain lift the trophy. Djed Spence remained with England until the third-place play-off on 18 July.Assuming players take the minimum three weeks off under Fifa guidelines, the players who reached the final would not return until 9 August, while Spence's earliest return date would be 8 August.That leaves them with around two weeks to reintegrate before their Premier League season begins at Brentford on 22 August.However, Spurs confirmed that Senesi - who made two World Cup appearances after being a late call-up for Argentina - was at the club's training ground for the first time on Thursday for pre-season testing.For managers, the challenge is not simply the absence itself. Players returning so late miss much of pre-season's tactical work, conditioning sessions and friendly matches, creating a difficult balancing act between preparation and recovery.Arsenal and Man City carry heaviest burdenManchester City and Arsenal, meanwhile, had the greatest concentration of players making deep runs into the competition.City's World Cup contingent featured for several of the tournament's leading nations.Rodri helped Spain win their second men's World Cup after playing 726 minutes, while Marc Guehi and Elliot Anderson helped England reach the final weekend. Nico O'Reilly featured in England's semi-final run, while Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku both reached the quarter-finals.Arsenal's numbers were similarly striking.Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka remained involved until England's 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off, while Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino reached the final with Spain. William Saliba helped France reach the third-place play-off, although he was subsequently injured and did not feature again. Noni Madueke was part of England's run to the final weekend but did not play beyond the quarter-finals, while Martin Odegaard captained Norway to the quarter-finals.The workload concerns are already being felt. City's Rodri recently had back surgery and is expected to miss a "short period" at the start of the season, while Saliba avoided surgery, but Arsenal have confirmed he will be sidelined for an "extended period" because of a back issue.Even though neither setback can be attributed solely to the World Cup, both underline the physical demands being placed on players in an increasingly crowded football calendar.Those clubs are likely to begin the campaign without having enjoyed a full pre-season with several key players.Little time to recoverThe World Cup's biggest workload belonged to Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who played all 810 minutes of Argentina's run to the final.Liverpool midfielder Alexis Mac Allister ranked second among Premier League players with 749 minutes, while Spain midfielder Rodri was third on 726.Several players effectively completed the equivalent of eight full matches during the tournament.Goalkeepers naturally face different physical demands from outfield players, but the figures underline the extent of Premier League involvement throughout the competition.With the players entitled to a minimum three-week break under Fifa regulations, for those involved in the final on 19 July - including Rodri, Porro, Zubimendi, Mac Allister, Enzo Fernandez, Emiliano Martinez and Lisandro Martinez - the earliest return date is 9 August.Players who featured in England's third-place play-off will return a day earlier.That leaves clubs with roughly 12 days to reintegrate some of their most important players before competitive football begins.Football's calendar shows no sign of easingThe concerns extend beyond this summer's World Cup.Many of football's leading players have now experienced three consecutive summers of major tournaments, following Euro 2024 and Copa America, then last year's expanded Club World Cup and now the World Cup.One of those players is Rodri, who warned in 2024 that footballers were "close" to striking because of workload concerns.Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca have also voiced concerns about the demands being placed on elite players and the growing number of matches in the calendar.The growing injury list during the World Cup provided another reminder of those concerns.Aston Villa midfielder Amadou Onana suffered a serious knee injury while representing Belgium, while Manchester United and Uruguay defensive midfielder Manuel Ugarte saw his tournament cut short by injury. Reece James also had his minutes carefully managed by England as he continued his recovery from a hamstring problem.For clubs such as Tottenham, Arsenal, Manchester City and Chelsea, the challenge is now immediate.The World Cup has concluded. The countdown to the Premier League season is under way.But for some players, recovery comes first, and the race to be ready for opening weekend has only just begun.

schema.headline: World Cup 2026: The Premier League clubs fighting a World Cup hangover

title: Franco Baresi: AC Milan and Italy great dies aged 66
description: Baresi formed part of one of European football's most celebrated defences alongside Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti. He also l
body: Baresi formed part of one of European football's most celebrated defences alongside Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti. He also lifted four Supercoppa Italianas, two European Super Cups and the Intercontinental Cup twice. In the 1994 World Cup, he returned from a knee injury to play in the final and largely nullified the threat of Brazil's Romario and Bebeto in a 0-0 draw.It was the first World Cup final to be decided by a shootout and Baresi missed the first penalty, with Brazil eventually winning it 3-2. Baresi had surgery in August 2025 to remove a lung nodule, and his last public appearance was at the San Siro Stadium for the Winter Olympics opening ceremony in February. In a statement on X, AC Milan wrote: "Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi. His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is." In a further post on the club's website,, external they added: "Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan is incredibly difficult. But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi's memory."In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he'll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever." Maldini, 58, who also spent his entire career at Milan, paid tribute to his former team-mate, writing on Instagram:, external "Today, I feel the same way I did whenever - for whatever reason - you couldn't take the field alongside us: how will we manage without our captain?"You taught me to fight until my very last breath, and showed me the meaning of devotion to the jersey and the true value of leadership."You protected me when I was a child, guided me as a young man, and inspired me as an adult. "You were the greatest footballer I ever had the honour of playing with."Former Italy goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon shared memories of his debut for Parma competing against Baresi as a 17-year-old in 1995. He wrote: "For a boy my age, finding myself on the field against champions like him was something incredible. From that day on, I had an even clearer understanding of what it meant to represent football with class, leadership and respect." Inter Milan said:, external "Farewell to Franco Baresi, protagonist of the great clashes in the Milan derby and one of the figures who most defined the history of the rivalry. "Captain, team man and flagbearer of AC Milan, he lived every match-up with Inter between competition and respect, within a challenge that wrote unforgettable pages of Italian soccer."Inter Milan manager Cristian Chivu said Baresi's death "is a sad day for the whole world, he represented being one of the greats in the history of football".Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni said Baresi "was not only one of the greatest champions in (Italian) sports history, but also an example of loyalty, seriousness, and dedication".The head of the Italian football federation (FICG), Giovanni Malago, praised Baresi for the "romantic choice" of staying loyal to AC Milan throughout his career, "which rightfully made him enter the hearts of the fans and millions of Italians."Everyone is hurting, it is a very sad day. Franco Baresi is a legend in Italy, one of the last so-called 'flags' - a one-club player, a player who has only worn one shirt for his entire career.After 15 years as AC Milan captain, his shirt had already been retired so no-one will ever wear the number six again - it shows how important he was for Milan, a symbol of the city.At AC Milan they called him 'Piscinin' - it means a fragile, thin youngster in Milan dialect. That was his nickname when he started back in the 1970s and it was given to him by a famous Italian journalist called Gianni Brera.He had a trial at Inter when he was 12 and his brother Beppe was already at the club, but they rejected him. He ended up at AC Milan that way. But even Inter are mourning, his value has been recognised by all opponents as he is a legend not only for AC Milan. Find me a fan who didn't like or recognise the value of Franco Baresi - it is not going to happen. That is how loved he was.He played alongside some of the biggest champions, Marco van Basten, Paolo Maldini, Ruud Gullit, Frank Rijkaard and he was always at the same level. Baresi was one of the immortal AC Milan players.He won three European Cups, but there were also some sad times - the World Cup in 1994 and the penalty miss. He couldn't play for much of the tournament given the injury he suffered at the beginning, but he made a speedy recovery to play a great game in the final against Brazil.To then miss a penalty in the shootout was a very sad moment for the whole of Italy. But we have never been angry, because Franco Baresi was one of the pillars of the team and the fact he recovered to play in the final was simply inhuman.And in 1989, he finished second in the Ballon d'Or to his team-mate Van Basten - back then, it was inconceivable a defender could win the Ballon d'Or, but Baresi got that close and deserved to win it for the player he was, the quality he had and all he represented - his leadership, importance, quality and his belonging to a club. He deserved that recognition.

schema.headline: Franco Baresi: AC Milan and Italy great dies aged 66

title: 'I pay £580 a month to live in a disused care home': Property guardians show us around
description: Image source, Moses KamangaImage caption, Katrina has been living in a former care home for 10 monthsByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterWould you live in
body: Image source, Moses KamangaImage caption, Katrina has been living in a former care home for 10 monthsByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterWould you live in a disused care home, pub or bank in exchange for a heavily discounted rent?  As cost of living pressures persist, a growing number of people are applying to become so-called property guardians - living in vacant residential or commercial buildings to protect them from squatters, vandalism and disrepair.They typically pay 30-50% less rent than private tenants, sometimes with bills thrown in, in exchange for looking after the buildings.However property guardians also have significantly fewer rights than private renters and can be evicted with just 28 days' notice.Katrina, 29, has spent the last 10 months living with around 50 other people in an Edwardian mansion in Hampstead, London, which was used as a care home until 2015.Image source, KatrinaImage caption, One of the communal living areas in Katrina's 50-person house shareThe postgraduate student, who says she could not afford to rent privately in the capital, currently pays £580 a month for her room including bills and council tax, about £400 below the London average, external. Katrina says guardianship gives her the chance to live in an unusual property and describes the mansion as an "incredible" and "romantic" place despite it being "quite run down". Set in 1.7 acres of gardens, the building has grand staircases, south-west-facing balconies and chandeliers in some rooms, but it does have some downsides: "We've had mushrooms growing on the walls, leaks, parts of the balcony stonework have fallen off," says Katrina.Image source, LOWEImage caption, The disused care home has high ceilings and large windowsKatrina says she loves the communal aspect of guardianship, which is "somewhere between living in university halls, a block of flats and a fancy squat".She lives with "all sorts of people", from lawyers to artists, sharing bathrooms, a kitchen and communal living areas, and regularly socialising.But there are disagreements over things like noise, she says. And while Lowe, the company that manages the property, operates a stringent vetting process for its guardians, two residents have been asked to leave because of antisocial behaviour - one for alleged sexual harassment. Lowe tells the BBC it acts "quickly and decisively" on the rare occasion someone breaches its standards and that the "overwhelming majority" of guardians go on to be "brilliant, community-minded residents".'It's really precarious'In general, guardians have fewer rights than private renters, external because they hold a "licence to occupy" rather than a tenancy. Guardianship companies are not obliged to protect their deposits or carry out repairs not specifically provided for in the agreement. Landlords can also visit at any time, without warning, and evict residents without giving a reason. Katrina admits she worries about the temporary nature of her arrangement sometimes. A developer bought the former care home last year and plans to turn it into flats, so she will eventually have to leave.  "It's really precarious in that sense. It's not guaranteed to last. If anyone doesn't like that, it's not for them," she says.Image source, David HaleImage caption, David Hale has lived in a disused school in South London for the last three yearsLast year, the Property Guardian Providers Association (PGPA) estimated there were between 10,000 and 15,000 property guardians in the UK, mainly in major cities, with most aged between 20 and 35.The trade group says the number of people applying has risen sharply as rental costs soar. David Hale, 32, became a guardian almost 10 years ago to save money and has never lived in standard rental accommodation.He and his wife now rent a "massive" space at a former primary school in Brixton, South London, for around £1,500 a month, including bills and council tax. He says they wouldn't be able to afford a similar property otherwise and save about £1,000 a month. Tips on becoming a property guardianPrepare to be flexible: You may stay for several years, or you may need to move on with relatively short notice.Choose an established guardian company: Look for a reputable provider with good health and safety proceduresRead your licence agreement carefully: Understand your responsibilities to the building, house rules and visitor policies Know your rights: Guardians are legally entitled to a court order before they can be evicted and their home must be safe to live inEmbrace community living: Be considerate of those you live with and respect shared areas.Sources: the Property Guardian Providers Association, Shelter, Ad Hoc Property ManagementImage source, David HaleImage caption, Large open classrooms have been converted into living spaceAround 20 guardians live in the school's open classrooms and offices, sharing a kitchen and large garden. But while David has enjoyed communal living, he and his wife are saving to buy their own home: "We wouldn't want to share toilets and bathrooms forever. We also want to start a family." The PGPA believes guardianship could help ease the UK's housing crisis by providing affordable temporary accommodation for thousands of people. It points out that over a million homes currently stand empty, along with tens of millions of square feet, external of non-residential property.But housing charity Shelter argues the rise of property guardianship shows how people are being forced "further and further afield just to keep a roof over their heads"."For most, this isn't a good alternative to an affordable, stable home," says chief executive Sarah Elliott. title: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m
description: Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for £120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food bu
body: Sainsbury's has agreed to sell Argos for £120m after a long process of trying to offload it as the supermarket chain aims to focus on its main food business.Sainsbury's said it would be "business as usual" for Argos customers, staff, and suppliers. Shoppers will see no change as Argos will still operate in Sainsbury's shops, sell Habitat products, and offer Nectar points.The buyer, Swift Partners, is a company that has been created to buy the brand  and includes former Co-operative Group boss Richard Pennycook.There are 667 Argos shops across the UK, with 201 operating as standalone stores and 466 operating within Sainsbury's. It also has more than 450 collection points.Founded in 1973, Argos opened shops where customers browsed its catalogues and placed their orders, with products being delivered to tills from warehouses connected to the stores.The Argos catalogue, once described by comedian Bill Bailey as the "laminated book of dreams", used to be a physical book.Argos no longer prints this hefty tome, with its full range now available online instead. In store, customers can browse the product collection on tablet computers.Sainsbury's has been trying to sell Argos - which has been seen as an underperforming brand - for some time.Sainsbury's bought Argos – together with Habitat and all the other retail brands owned by Home Retail Group – in 2016 for £1.4bn. It then sold Argos financial services, which runs the Argos card, for around £720m in 2024.In September last year, its talks to sell the rest of Argos to Chinese online retailer JD.com fell through.Sainsbury's chief executive Simon Roberts said that all of Argos's nearly 14,000 staff would be transferred over to Swift Partners as part of the deal.He also confirmed that Argos would continue to operate in Sainsbury's shops; Nectar will continue to be used across both Argos and Sainsbury's; and Sainsbury's will continue to sell Habitat productsSwift Partners' Pennycook said he believed "strongly in Argos's future and see real opportunities to invest and build on its progress".The deal is expected to be completed in February next year.Pennycook said there was the potential to open new standalone Argos shops – and did not rule out the possibility of the return of its print catalogue.Retail expert Catherine Shuttleworth said Argos has been a "distraction" from Sainsbury's main food business.She said having new owners focused entirely on it gives Argos the potential to be a "really digital-first business".She praised the user-friendliness of its app and said its click-and-collect model, where customers can order something online and pick it up from an Argos shop the same day, means it can give a "bloody nose" to online retail giants like Amazon.Retail analyst Clive Black said he had always questioned whether Argos was "wholly aligned" with Sainsbury's grocery business, describing the supermarket group's attempt to sell Argos as "challenging and prolonged".He said Argos has been a "suboptimal performer from a financial perspective".In Sainsbury's latest results for the first three months of this year, group-wide sales were up 3.1%, although sales for Argos specifically had dipped 0.5%.Bally Auluk, national officer at Usdaw, a union which represents Argos workers, said the announcement would create uncertainty, but that it welcomed Swift's commitment to "keeping the model of store in stores, standalone stores and local fulfilment centres".

schema.headline: Sainsbury's agrees to sell Argos for £120m

title: Glasgow gets starring role in Spider-Man: Brand New Day film
description: Image source, Marvel/ Sony Pictures EntertainmentImage caption, Glasgow doubled as New York City in the latest Spider-Man movieByNichola RutherfordBBC
body: Image source, Marvel/ Sony Pictures EntertainmentImage caption, Glasgow doubled as New York City in the latest Spider-Man movieByNichola RutherfordBBC ScotlandUpdated 4 hours agoAny comic book fan knows that Spider-Man's secret identity is Peter Parker, a science nerd who gained superhero powers after being bitten by a radioactive spider. But in the latest installment from the Marvel cinematic universe, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Parker - played by Tom Holland - is not the only star in disguise. The action takes place in New York City but much of the movie, which premiered in London this week, was filmed more than 3,000 miles away in Glasgow.Filming almost brought the city centre to a halt last summer, when fans gathered to watch Holland in an action sequence in full superhero mode. Parts of the nearby Merchant City were also dressed up to resemble the Big Apple. It was the latest in a long line of Hollywood blockbusters to have been filmed in the city in recent years. And next month Glasgow is expected to double as Gotham City, when filming starts on the sequel to The Batman. Screen Scotland said the Victorian architecture, wide avenues and grid layout make it an "incredibly versatile stand-in" for many US cities. Figure caption, Tom Holland filming new Spider-Man film in GlasgowFilmmaker Destin Daniel Cretton praised Scotland as a filming destination during an interview at the premiere on Wednesday."I love Scotland," he told Press Association. "I got to go to Scotland first ages ago with a short film to the Edinburgh Film Festival and I fell in love with that place."The 37-year-old added: "When we shot in Glasgow, that was our first day shooting and that was just such an energising way to start."We had thousands of people show up who are cheering us on and getting excited and feeling that energy which was really a wonderful way to start."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Crowds of people watched the filming in GlasgowImage source, PA MediaImage source, PA MediaAsked about what would draw him back to Scotland, Cretton said: "The people. The people in Glasgow, in particular, were so warm and welcoming and fun and knew how to party and have a good time."It was a really wonderful experience."Producer Amy Pascal said "everything about Scotland is great" and that it was "wonderful to make movies in the real places".The film follows Parker as he navigates his new life four years on from the events of the last film, 2021's Spider-Man: No Way Home, which saw a spell cast to make the world forget his real identity so he can save the universe.His romance with MJ (Zendaya) and his friendship with Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) have also been erased from civilians' minds, leaving a lonely Peter to continue his crime-fighting in secret while his friends experience life at university.Image source, Marvel/ Sony Pictures EntertainmentImage caption, Glasgow's streets are the backdrop to the filmImage source, Marvel/Sony Pictures EntertainmentImage caption, Streets in Glasgow can be spotted in an early chase scene in the movieImage source, Marvel/ Sony Pictures EntertainmentScreen Scotland, which supports Scotland's film and TV industry, said: "It's fantastic to see Spiderman: Brand New Day hitting our screens."As we can already see from the trailer, Glasgow has a starring role, as the city once again seamlessly doubles for New York. "Glasgow's grid layout,  wide avenues and Victorian architecture make it an incredibly versatile stand-in for many US cities including New York and Philadelphia and Spiderman: Brand New Day is the latest example of the scale of production the city can accommodate."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The centre of Glasgow was transformed during the filming in 2025Image source, PA MediaImage source, PA Media

schema.headline: Glasgow gets starring role in Spider-Man: Brand New Day film

title: Gianni Infantino 'wrong man' to lead Fifa says Prime Minister Andy Burnham
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Gianni Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa after a senior adviser to the president resigned and a third confed
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Gianni Infantino was "the wrong man" to lead Fifa after a senior adviser to the president resigned and a third confederation opposed his plan to sell stakes in competitions to private investors.Burnham was critical of the proposal when it was first announced, and told reporters on Friday: "This was an outrageous suggestion."The idea that it could even be brought forward shows that, in my view, [he] is the wrong man to lead the organisation."Burnham was speaking hours after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said it "stands in solidarity" with counterparts in Europe and North, Central America and the Caribbean.The AFC added Infantino's plan could not "realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and unity required to move forward"."The Fifa World Cup is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all Confederations and the world's leading football nations," it said."Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered."Shortly after that statement, Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - resigned, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".The AFC's statement means Infantino's plans are unlikely to be approved by Fifa members if put to a vote.Infantino had indicated the proposals would need a straight majority to go through - meaning 106 of its 211 members needed to vote in favour for the proposal.Uefa - the body that governs European football - has 55 votes. Concacaf, which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, has 35 and Asia has 46.Should all member associations back the stance of their governing body, that would mean 136 nations are against Infantino's plan.In its statement, the AFC accused Fifa of once again setting the "direction of travel" for a "significant initiative" before consulting stakeholders.It said Fifa's failure to consult its member associations on the proposals had "exposed fundamental weaknesses in Fifa's consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed".The AFC also criticised Fifa for leaving "confederations, member associations and even Fifa's own governing bodies, including the Fifa Council, feeling sidelined."It added: "The Fifa  World Cup, and the game itself, belong to the entire global football family."Their future must always be shaped collectively, through institutions that reflect the voices of all Confederations and member associations."The AFC calls upon Fifa to undertake an urgent review of its governance and decision-making framework to ensure that proposals of global significance are developed through proper consultation, meaningful engagement and appropriate oversight by Fifa's statutory bodies."Cordeiro had been a Fifa senior adviser for four years and 11 months.He represented the world governing body on the White House taskforce for the 2026 World Cup and was a former investment banker with Goldman Sachs.Appointed in September 2021, he is the first senior figure at Fifa to resign over the plans.In a lengthy statement, Cordeiro said he "unequivocally" opposed the plans and said he "did not accept the proposition" Fifa needed outside investors to "unlock greater value"."The proposal has become a defining question for Fifa's future," he wrote."Fifa's responsibility is not to maximise commercial returns at any cost. It is to protect and strengthen football for future generations."When those principles come into conflict, football must come first."Cordeiro said he had no involvement in this proposal."Most troubling of all is the absence of answers to fundamental questions," he added. "Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits?" he wrote."These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet member associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind. "That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game."Fifa and Infantino want to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.It said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).In a 25-page document created by investment bank JP Morgan, it is made clear Fifa's tournaments would expand to hit an estimated increased pay-out of 24m euros per member association in the 2035-2039 cycle.It mentions "new business initiatives" and "attracting top talent with incentive-driven compensation".The World Cup is described in it as the "most widely viewed" sporting event but Fifa, by contrast, is said to be "under-monetised".There is no mention in the document of the women's game.If approval is granted, Fifa says Thrive Eternal is expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.On Thursday, Uefa voted to boycott World Cups if the Fifa plan proceeded.Hours later, Concacaf, which hosted this year's World Cup, released a statement also rejecting the proposals made by Infantino.Fifa released a statement early on Friday vowing to continue with the plan - but added "nobody is selling football".The governing body of world football claimed the consultation process had been "disrupted by incorrect media reports".It claimed that would "not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of Fifa or football itself".Uefa has accused Fifa of using football "to enrich themselves and their friends", while Concacaf and AFC have both expressed concerns about consultation over the plans."The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product," Uefa's statement on Thursday read."It is one of football's greatest sporting legacies. It has been built over generations by players, national teams and supporters across every continent."No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.The governing body overseeing football in South America, Conmebol, is yet to publicly comment on the proposals. The governing bodies in Africa (CAF) and Oceania (OFC) have said they will discuss Fifa's plan in August.While Uefa members are among the richest on the planet, many other nations rely on Fifa funding for basic infrastructure.While the AFC opposes Infantino's plan, unlike Uefa it has not threatened to boycott Fifa competitions. AFC members would not be obliged to vote against the proposals. Rogers Byamukama, of the Ugandan Football Federation, argued any avenue that could lead to more resources for nations like his should be explored."First and foremost, you need to understand that football is a very expensive venture, especially on the African continent where the resources are not easy to come by," he told Newsday on BBC World Service."For instance in Uganda, the number of infrastructure projects that have been funded by Fifa from the resources generated by Fifa, especially at the World Cup, both from ticket sales as well as sponsors."On top of that, there are many grassroots programmes that have been funded by Fifa, including schools for football."From my perspective, any avenue that brings in more resources is good because those resources would be distributed and given to federations, especially on the African continent and that would inspire growth."Byamukama acknowledged Uefa's right to speak out, but suggested its members were not reliant on Fifa funding like many associations in the rest of the world where Infantino remains popular.In the first two cycles of the Fifa Forward development programme, through to 2022, $2.8bn (£2.08bn) was made available for investment across the 211 member associations.Fifa Forward 3.0 - covering the years 2023 through to 2026 - has produced a 30% increase in funding.Fifa has provided a further $5m (£3.7m) for every member association, with another $60m (£44.48m) paid to each confederation for their own projects.After expanding the men's World Cup to 48 teams from 32 for the 2026 edition, Fifa is seeking an independent agency to assess an expansion to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament.The timeline on documents seen by BBC Sport said Fifa would receive agency proposals by 7 August, with a Fifa decision on 14 August. Delivery of analysis by the agency is then scheduled for 11 September.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino 'wrong man' to lead Fifa says Prime Minister Andy Burnham

title: Scottish Premiership: Will it return to a two-team title tussle?
description: And in the relative blink of an eye, the new Scottish Premiership season is upon us with much to live up to compared to last time, an epic campaign th
body: And in the relative blink of an eye, the new Scottish Premiership season is upon us with much to live up to compared to last time, an epic campaign that looked like making the impossible possible for month upon month.How Scotland, and other parts of the world, became entranced by the fairytale only for the reality of sport's essential brutality to hit them square between the eyes at Celtic Park on denouement day.If there is a non-Glasgow team capable of roughing up the big two as Heart of Midlothian did repeatedly last season then we're in for a wild ride.If this league campaign goes to the final three minutes on the final day, if the domestic football story to beat all domestic football stories is in touching distance as the campaign swings for home next spring then we'll be blessed.If. Nobody will be betting a brass farthing on history repeating itself, though. True, nobody really saw Hearts coming last time, but does lightning strike twice?Hearts are in transition under new management and a raft of new players in the post-Derek McInnes, Lawrence Shankland age. They'll take time to settle.Is there a different bolter out there? Motherwell, so easy on the eye last season, have had their guts ripped out in the summer and are also rebuilding, albeit playing with the same easy style as before.Aberdeen? It would take a brave soul to support any claim for an Old Firm-challenging run, but in Stephen Robinson's first full season, they should go a whole lot better than last term.Hibernian have the potential to push hard for third, but consistency problems follow them around year upon year. Falkirk, the other top-six club, would see a repeat of last season as a fantastic outcome, which it would be.The plaintive cry is that young Scottish footballers get a chance to play a part in all this, that clubs trust their youth for a change. It's an appeal made this time every year and, for the most part, ignored.We look to be back in the realms of a two-horse race and the two horses have experienced jockeys now, not two Old Firm apprentices like Russell Martin and Wilfried Nancy.Hearts did so many outstanding things in taking the race to the wire, but both of those hapless characters helped them on their way. In Martin O'Neill and McInnes, the capacity for Celtic and Rangers slapstick, and that of an outsider causing them tremors, has been dramatically reduced.The surreal cameos of Martin and Nancy and Hearts' thrilling surge that reverberated around the UK, Europe and parts of the wider world were just a few of things that made last season unmatchable in terms of drama and genuine gobsmacking moments.The fall of Brendan Rodgers, and Dermot Desmond's startling evisceration of a celebrated manager, could only be rivalled if Celtic's major shareholder suddenly takes a flamethrower to his relationship with O'Neill.Desmond's son, Ross, thought it a good idea to declare football war on the club's own supporters at an annual meeting that was promptly cancelled. On the really dark side, Peter Lawwell, the titan of 20 years at Parkhead, left while citing intolerable abuse of a section of the support that lost the run of themselves.O'Neill's return was astonishing, his second return almost every bit as remarkable. Danny Rohl came and went at Rangers. Jimmy Thelin exited Aberdeen. St Mirren won a League Cup in thrilling circumstances and then almost got themselves relegated. Everybody fell in love with Jens Berthel Askou's Motherwell. Praise was heaped on the quality of Falkirk's football.At the start of the season nobody foresaw much, if any, of this. What was more predictable then, as it is now, is the toxic nature of some of what goes around the biggest games. As a club, Hearts have every right to remain livid at the crass goading of their players during the invasion that greeted Celtic's title win - and the tokenistic sanction that followed it.The Scottish FA's independent review of the disgraceful scenes before, during and after the Old Firm Cup tie at Ibrox in March was thunderously critical of all parties - clubs, governing bodies, police.Their recommendation, one of many, was that the SFA and Scottish Professional Football League start to get serious with stand closures and then stadium closures as a direct consequence of misbehaviour. Enough is enough was the mantra.How long before the mettle of the governing bodies is tested? And how long before the independent report, in the face of resistance from the most powerful clubs in the land, is quietly forgotten about? In the coming seasons, the narratives don't just begin and end on the pitch. The off-pitch stuff is compelling, too.The standards of refereeing will be under the microscope like never before after the contentious and title-defining calls came in a mad flurry at the end of last season. We want the drama and the storylines of much of the campaign just gone, but we could do without the poisonous way it all finished in the final week or two.Controversial decisions, threats to officials, a noxious atmosphere culminating with Celtic fans squaring up to Hearts players -  it was a pitiful end to what been a thrilling season.There will be surprises ahead, but at this remove it's hard to argue against the familiar sight of old rivals going head-to-head for the title.The Celtic board spent much of last season and practically every day of the summer getting monstered by elements among their own support. They have, though, delivered two significant signings for huge money - Kasper Hogh and Camilo Duran. Hogh is the pedigree striker that Celtic have lacked since Kyogo Furuhashi was around. Duran is more of a replacement for Daizen Maeda. At a reported £17m for the pair, Celtic have flexed their fiscal muscle.There is consistent talk that midfielder Arne Engels and right-back Alistair Johnston might be leaving, so the Celtic of this week might still look considerably different to the Celtic of the coming months. Even with another few comings and goings they're still the most settled side in the country - and the most proven. Fit-again centre-half Cameron Carter-Vickers will be like a new signing. If winger Jota can make a return to something close to his old self then Celtic will be hard to contain.Rangers, under McInnes, have added beef and leadership, doughty characters rather than the flighty articles they have been attracted to for so long. McInnes will make them organised and robust. Whether they have the creative wit to go with the physicality is another question. In Scottish terms, Rangers' American owners have spent colossal money, splurging tens of millions on the creation of a team, and an environment, that can win a league and do something in Europe.From Martin's capricious management to the cold-blooded pragmatism of McInnes is some leap for Rangers. McInnes has broad shoulders, which is just as well, because there's a heavy burden of expectation there. There's enormous pressure on him.He'll see it as an opportunity, of course. The biggest of his managerial life. O'Neill versus McInnes looks to be the story of the season, unless there's another delicious sub-plot lurking in the long grass.

schema.headline: Scottish Premiership: Will it return to a two-team title tussle?

title: Millions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?
description: Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, Mae Sot has become home to so many who left Myanmar to oppose the junta - and their future is increasingly u
body: Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, Mae Sot has become home to so many who left Myanmar to oppose the junta - and their future is increasingly uncertainByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondent and Lulu LuoSouth East Asia producer Reporting fromMae Sot, Thailand"One day we will get our freedom back."The 22-year-old has spent much of his adult life fighting for it. But now, after five years of civil war in Myanmar, he has had enough of war and political struggle."I want to help our people as much as I can. But I choose another way. A non-violent way."The young man is part of a huge exodus of people from Myanmar seeking sanctuary in the Thai border town of Mae Sot.He spoke to the BBC from a small, dark room tucked away down a back street – one of a network of safe houses set up by charities to help new arrivals. Most have very little. They are exhausted, traumatised by their experiences in Myanmar, and very vulnerable. With no legal status in Thailand, the safe houses are their only refuge.He was 17 when he joined the nationwide protests against the military coup in Myanmar in 2021.When these were crushed by the army, like many young protesters he travelled to an area controlled by ethnic insurgents to get military training.He returned to Yangon as part of an urban guerrilla squad, planting bombs outside targets like police stations. "I thought then that non-violent protests were not the right way to get back our freedom."But he was soon caught and sentenced to seven years in Insein prison, notorious for its brutal treatment of inmates. He was released last year, and fled to Mae Sot because of the intense police surveillance of his family at their home in Yangon. It is for their sake that he does not want to use his name.For the millions of Burmese who have risked their lives and left their homes to oppose military rule, these are disheartening times.They have been dreaming of a revolution which will remake Myanmar as a more democratic and inclusive country, and purge the armed forces from politics.Instead, they are watching the man they hold responsible for igniting the civil war strengthen his hold on power.Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, Exhausted by war, the 22-year-old says he wants to choose a "non-violent" way to helpLast month Myanmar's military ruler General Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome by China's Xi Jinping, capping a joint effort by both countries to transform his image from blood-stained dictator to civilian president, increasingly accepted, if not respected, by neighbouring countries.Chinese diplomatic and military support has been critical in helping the man who deposed the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021 to recover from the catastrophic consequences of his coup. Over the past year the military junta recaptured much of the territory it had lost to the hundreds of insurgent groups which formed to resist the coup.A stage-managed election earlier this year, from which the main opposition groups were excluded, has now allowed Min Aung Hlaing to present himself as a legitimate, elected leader.So where does that leave those who had hoped for a very different future? Many are effectively trapped in Mae Sot.The town is the main gateway for trade between Myanmar and Thailand, and has always had a large, though fluctuating Burmese population. This has been swollen by refugees since the coup. But you rarely see them outside.Most are undocumented. They got here unofficially, by crossing the narrow Moei river which marks the border, and live in constant fear of arrest and deportation by the Thai police. They also fear reprisals against family members back in Myanmar. One former army officer, who defected to the opposition three years ago, told the BBC she only dares leave the room she rents in Mae Sot twice a month.For those who have just arrived, the safe houses offer them short-term shelter, usually for a maximum of six months. These are warrens of small rooms with basic communal facilities, hidden down the city's smaller side-streets. Behind every door is a harrowing personal story.Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, The tiny, bare rooms in Mae Sot's safe houses are a temporary refuge for those fleeing MyanmarThe young urban guerilla who was imprisoned in Insein jail described routine torture and sexual assault by the guards. He also says prison was where he had a change of heart about the struggle."I had hoped the revolution would be better. But they did not unite at all [the insurgent groups], they fought each other and I did not like that situation. I saw many casualties from the war, and I could not bear to see things like that."As the eldest child, he also felt he couldn't risk his life and abandon his family. "So I gave up the armed struggle – not only the armed struggle but other kinds of struggle too, like in politics. I want to help our people in another way."He has dedicated himself to teaching children in the safe house, and to supporting as best he can friends who are still in prison."I try to give them hope that the revolution is not finished yet, and that we still have a chance to win."Our presence in the safe house drew a crowd of other residents, all with different stories to tell.There were former members of the people's defence forces which have been fighting against the junta. There was an official from Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy, and several young men avoiding forced conscription into the army. A common refrain among them was that, while they all still believed in the revolution, after five years they were exhausted and needed to earn money for their families. Mae Sot was their only option.Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, A calendar with the image of deposed leader Aung San Suu Kyi at a local shopAlso here was Yin Yin Aung, a 20-year-old woman with her husband and young son. They had made an epic, 1,000-mile  journey to reach Mae Sot from Sagaing, a region which has put up some of the strongest resistance to the military coup, and suffered terrible reprisals, including relentless air strikes.Her village, Htomar, was sandwiched between a military base and an insurgent-controlled area. She described the day more than two years ago when soldiers occupied the village, firing their weapons and driving the population ahead of them."When the phone signal was cut, we knew something was going to happen. I heard three gunshots, and saw people running between the houses shouting that an army column was coming. We could not carry much. My father took a bag of rice so we would have something to eat, and we ran until we reached a place deep in the forest and hills."There was nothing there, she adds, so they had to drink the river water, which they also used for bathing, and as a toilet. They fell sick and some of them died. But they stayed in the forest for six months.The soldiers left the village after one month, but Yin Yin says it had been thoroughly looted, with landmines laid around the houses. No-one dared move back.During this time she gave birth to her son, but he has an abdominal hernia which needs surgery. Over several weeks the family made their way south and east, arriving six months ago in Mae Sot. This is the second safe house they have lived in; they had reached the maximum stay allowed in the first. They are trying to avoid having to rent a room commercially so she can save up for her son's operation.Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, Yin Yin Aung, with her toddler son, who needs surgery Not everyone is disheartened by the military's successes. In another safe house we met a former Yangon bartender-turned-rebel, with his wife and two month-old-baby. They had left war-torn Karen State, where he is a member of the Cobra Column, one of the more effective fighting units in the opposition, and come to Mae Sot to have their baby. But he seemed eager to get back to the war."I believe that the revolution we are fighting right now will succeed one day. Because they [the military] are fighting a war against the entire country. They are fighting a war against the very citizens they are supposed to protect and safeguard. There is no way they can win."Image source, BBC/ Jonathan HeadImage caption, This former resistance fighter believes the junta's victories are short-livedThe Cobra Column fights alongside the Karen National Union, which is relatively well-armed and has been fighting the central government for nearly 80 years. Morale is still high there. But other people's defence forces are struggling this year, after Chinese pressure cut their supplies of weapons and technology. Meanwhile the Myanmar military has benefitted from training and new equipment from Russia and China.Louis – not his real name – is an entrepreneur from Yangon, who left to join the insurgents in Karen State after the coup."I thought it was my duty as a citizen, even though I was already 40-something years old. I thought if I don't join now, I will regret it for the rest of my life."He too was captured and imprisoned by the military junta, but was able to persuade them he was an ethnic Karen combatant, not a member of the civil disobedience movement that emerged in response to the coup. That at least meant he got treated less harshly. But when he was released last year, he decided his family's need was greater than that of the revolution."For the first two or three years, we had high morale and were very motivated. But, since the war is dragging on for so long, a lot of people have other responsibilities that do not stop. Like me, my kids are growing up, they need a good education, a better life. A lot of people feel like this. We have changed under that pressure."Many of those recruited to fight in Myanmar's civil war are children as young as 13. One activist has dedicated herself to extracting them from insurgent groups, and bringing them to a refuge she has made in an old house in Mae Sot, where she tries to get them work experience. The adjustment is hard. The youngest boys have become conditioned to military life, and still have family members fighting on the other side of the border. They feel it is their duty to be with them."Sometimes I get depressed about the revolution," she says. "Before the coup there were villages which were friends, and now they become enemies because one supports the military and another supports the resistance."She believes it's time for them to change their strategy. "We have to prepare for a long fight for this revolution, not only with weapons, but also thinking about education and healthcare. There are many displaced people now in refugee camps. What are we going to do for them?"Yin Yin Aung has been told by a private hospital in Mae Sot she must raise a deposit of 38,000 baht (about $1,140; £845) for her son's operation, a near impossible sum for her and her husband. Without any official status they have no access to Thailand's state-run health system. Ideally, she would like to go back to her village, but says that so long as Min Aung Hlaing is in charge, she must stay in Thailand."He is the very one who caused all of this to happen. So, if you ask whether we could live there with him still in power, we cannot. Because given the choice, I would prefer to bring my parents here."Image source, BBC/ Lulu LuoImage caption, Many of those from Myanmar reach Mae Sot by illegally crossing the narrow Moei river on the borderDespite shedding his uniform Min Aung Hlaing is not letting up on his war against the opposition. Last month the UN Human Rights Commissioner reported that a minimum of 702 civilian deaths had occurred in the period between the election announcement last August and its conclusion at the end of January, most of them women and children, most killed by air strikes.Fragmented among hundreds of armed groups and starved of arms, the resistance has lost ground in recent months, but still controls large parts of the country. And yet diplomatic engagement by Myanmar's neighbours has so far produced no meaningful concessions from the regime.All of this leaves hundreds of thousands of Myanmar's war refugees, including those in Mae Sot, in devastating limbo.  Yin Yin Aung's home is now a small, dimly lit room with a very basic bathroom at the back. It isn't much for a family of three. Those in the other 19 rooms are living in the same conditions, all carrying the weight of their own terrible memories of the war. With no end to her exile in Mae Sot in sight, in six months Yin Yin Aung will probably have to move again.

schema.headline: Millions opposed military rule in Myanmar. Is their dream of a revolution over?
